A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Safety Mirage study. Text extraction and visual inspection support comparison of the main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices despite extensive formatting and numbering changes.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLaVA safety and unlearning experiments, including attack success rates, rejection rates, VQA accuracy, token-saliency analyses, and visual-perturbation results.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds SPA-VL preference-aligned model diagnostics and experiments varying the amount of safety training data.

M1.justification: The stated retain objective changes substantially. v1 uses standard cross-entropy on retained data; v2 introduces a composite objective in Equation 4, adding representation matching for RMU and a reference-relative preference loss for NPO in Appendix C. The unsafe-data objectives remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions cover VLGuard, SPA-VL, MM-SafetyBench, FigStep, VQAv2, TextVQA, ScienceQA, and VizWiz. The additional preference-aligned checkpoints and data-subset experiments retain the existing safety and VQA tasks; they do not establish new domain or population coverage.

E2.justification: Direct unlearning comparisons retain the original model, Unsafe-Filter, Mixed-SFT, and Posthoc-SFT in the matched benchmark and response-decomposition tables. The newly examined SPA-VL DPO/PPO checkpoints are attack targets and diagnostic cases, rather than additional methods compared directly against unlearning.

E3.justification: v2 adds random 50%, 25%, and 10% safety-data training subsets and evaluations of SPA-VL DPO/PPO-30K checkpoints, using dataset-specific starting words. The existing three-shot ASR, one-shot benign-query RR, VQA metrics, and reported full/LoRA training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds SPA-VL word-frequency analysis, DPO/PPO case studies, and PPO attack/over-prudence curves in Figure 3 and Appendices A–B. Appendix D.4 adds a substantive data-fraction sensitivity study of the safety–utility tradeoff. The existing VLGuard shot analyses, saliency analyses, and visual-perturbation tests are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The existing token-saliency distribution plots are retained; additional attack attempts and training subsets do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds results on preference-aligned models and the safety–utility effects of reduced training data. For example, its full-data versus 10%-data RMU results report post-attack VLGuard ASR of 10.18% versus 22.12% and VQAv2 accuracy of 77.04% versus 78.32%, under different training budgets. Tables 1–2 and the matched original appendix benchmark tables retain their numerical values.

T1.justification: Equation 4 and Appendix C Equations A1–A2 introduce mathematical definitions of the composite retain objective and its method-specific penalties. The generic optimization problem and unsafe-data losses are retained. No new theoretical guarantees, theorems, or proofs are provided.

C1.justification: The central claims remain that textual spurious correlations cause safety mirage, enable one-word jailbreaks and over-prudence, and can be mitigated through machine unlearning while largely preserving utility. The headline reductions of 60.17% and 84.20% are retained. The expanded title emphasizes mitigation already claimed in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking SPA-VL token frequency and preference optimization to rejection behavior, motivates the composite loss through instability concerns, and interprets the coreset tradeoff. It also adds explicit model-scale and benchmark limitations, strengthens interpretations of visual robustness, and replaces v1's specific guardrail-removal misuse discussion with a broader benefits-and-risks discussion.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the composite-loss coefficient as alpha = 1 and more explicitly documents rejection filtering followed by relevance judging for ASR. It expands the Unsafe-Filter pipeline description and changes the code-link repository name from VLM-Safety-MU to VLM-Safety-Unlearn. Most hardware and optimization details, and the judging prompt, are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Pal et al. (2025) to motivate coreset unlearning and removes several unlearning and spurious-correlation references, including MM-SpuBench and RAVL. Section 4 drops the explicit novelty contrast with earlier visual-feature studies. The overall positioning of unlearning as mitigation for safety-data shortcuts remains.

P1.justification: Existing paragraphs throughout the introduction, problem statement, method, and results are extensively rewritten and condensed. The title expands, appendices are reorganized from A–B into A–F, broader impacts move out of the main text, and separate limitations and LLM-use sections appear.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a single-column preprint layout, redraws and relocates numerous displays, expands Figure 3, and adds appendix diagnostic figures and a coreset table. v1 Figure A1 becomes main-text Figure 5. The retained appendix benchmark tables are relabeled as Figures A4 and A7, although prose still calls them tables.

improvement.justification: The SPA-VL diagnostics strengthen the empirical support, and the coreset study quantifies a safety–utility tradeoff that v1 left to future work. More explicit loss and evaluation descriptions and stated limitations also help. These gains are limited by reporting inconsistencies: Appendix D.4 says smaller subsets increase RR, whereas Table A1 shows several decreases. The revision improves understanding without strengthening the retained main benchmark results.
